description: Independently authored cross-disciplinary gravitational-wave paleontology practice sets. Explanations and toy cases are educational, not new lab data or calibrated examinations.

sets.title: Binary orbits and binding energy
sets.summary: Relate orbital energy, angular momentum, period, eccentricity and survival without confusing one body's speed with relative motion.

objectives.title: Interpret energy and eccentricity
objectives.evidence: Separate bound Keplerian orbits, total orbital energy, and orbital shape.

questions.prompt: In the Newtonian point-mass two-body problem, a bound elliptical orbit has which relative mechanical energy?
choices: Positive
Negative
Exactly zero
questions.hint: Use the gravitational potential energy convention U(∞)=0.
questions.feedback: Relative orbital energy is negative for bound ellipses; zero is the parabolic threshold and positive corresponds to hyperbolic unbound motion.

questions.prompt: Two bound binaries have the same component masses and semi-major axis but different eccentricities. Their Keplerian orbital energies are:
choices: Different because an eccentric orbit always has more binding energy
Equal
Undetermined without the period
questions.hint: Recall E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) for point masses.
questions.feedback: At fixed masses and semi-major axis, total Keplerian orbital energy is equal even though angular momentum and speed as a function of position differ.

questions.prompt: A test particle passes through pericentre on a bound eccentric Keplerian orbit. Which statement is supported?
choices: Its total orbital energy suddenly increases at pericentre.
Its orbital speed is greatest there, although its total orbital energy is constant.
Its radial velocity is largest at pericentre.
questions.hint: Use energy conservation and the fact that separation is smallest at pericentre.
questions.feedback: A smaller separation corresponds to a more negative potential energy and larger kinetic energy; the radial velocity vanishes at a turning point.

objectives.title: Calculate energies and speeds
objectives.evidence: Interpret E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) and the vis-viva relation with correct held-fixed quantities.

questions.prompt: For the same component masses, a circular binary's semi-major axis halves. Its binding-energy magnitude changes by what factor?
choices: It halves.
It doubles.
It quadruples.
questions.hint: Binding-energy magnitude is proportional to 1/a.
questions.feedback: |E|=Gm₁m₂/(2a); halving a doubles |E| under the stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: A test body's circular orbital speed at radius r around a fixed central point mass M satisfies which relation?
choices: v²=GMr
v²=GM/r
v²=GM/r²
questions.hint: Balance GMm/r² with mv²/r.
questions.feedback: The centripetal acceleration is v²/r, giving v²=GM/r. G M/r² instead has acceleration units.

questions.prompt: Two point masses stay fixed while semi-major axis increases from a to 2a. E₂/E₁ equals:
questions.hint: Write both total orbital energies with their negative signs.
questions.feedback: E₂=−Gm₁m₂/(4a), E₁=−Gm₁m₂/(2a), hence E₂/E₁=1/2: the final orbit is less tightly bound.

objectives.title: Reason about sudden orbital changes
objectives.evidence: Use instantaneous separation, relative velocity and final masses to reason about a bound or unbound outcome.

questions.prompt: At an instantaneous symmetric mass-loss event, which quantities determine the immediately post-event point-mass relative orbital energy?
choices: The kick magnitude alone
Post-event total mass, separation and relative speed
Only the pre-event orbital period
questions.hint: Use ε=v_rel²/2−G M_after/r.
questions.feedback: The sign of ε depends jointly on post-event gravitational mass and the relative orbit at the event, not on one speed alone.

questions.prompt: Two identical pre-event binaries lose equal mass at different phases of their eccentric orbits. Why can outcomes differ?
choices: Eccentric orbits have no conserved energy.
Instantaneous separation and relative speed differ by orbital phase.
Mass loss always unbinds every eccentric binary.
questions.hint: Evaluate the energy immediately after the event using each event's r and v_rel.
questions.feedback: For equal mass changes, different event-phase values of r and relative velocity can change post-event energy and eccentricity.

questions.prompt: An initially bound binary receives a kick that reduces its relative speed, with masses and instantaneous separation fixed. Its immediate relative orbital energy:
choices: Must become positive.
Decreases (becomes more negative).
Is unchanged because the period has not updated.
questions.hint: Only the kinetic term changes at that instant.
questions.feedback: ε=v_rel²/2−GM/r: lowering speed lowers kinetic energy at fixed gravitational potential, while the new orbit can then be computed.

objectives.title: Check limits of the orbital model
objectives.evidence: Identify when simplified Keplerian formulae do not by themselves justify a physical conclusion.

questions.prompt: Can the circular-orbit relation v²=GM/r determine the speed at every point of an eccentric orbit?
choices: Yes; only r matters and energy is identical for every orbit.
No; use an eccentric-orbit relation such as vis-viva.
No; speed on an eccentric orbit is always constant.
questions.hint: Ask whether the trajectory is constrained to be circular.
questions.feedback: For an eccentric orbit, v²=GM(2/r−1/a) for relative motion; its semi-major axis also matters.

questions.prompt: Why is a remnant's velocity in the observer's frame insufficient to decide whether the binary survives?
choices: The observer's frame determines the gravitational constant.
Binding depends on the companion-relative velocity, masses and separation.
A positive absolute velocity makes every orbit unbound.
questions.hint: Switch to relative orbital coordinates.
questions.feedback: Bulk centre-of-mass motion can change individual frame velocities without changing the internal bound/unbound state.

questions.prompt: When using Keplerian orbital energy for a common-envelope interaction, what limitation should be stated?
choices: The point-mass formula exactly captures all envelope hydrodynamics.
Gas drag, mass exchange and energy transfer can invalidate isolated two-point-mass conservation during the interaction.
Conservation of energy never applies to gas.
questions.hint: Distinguish total energy conservation from constancy of the binary orbital energy alone.
questions.feedback: The orbital energy can transfer into gas and heat; isolated binary orbital energy need not remain constant during dissipative envelope evolution.

cases.title: Energy at a supernova
cases.scenario: A pre-event binary has r=1 (toy units), relative speed v=1, and post-event GM=0.6. Define ε=v²/2−GM/r.
cases.task: Compute ε and decide whether the post-event point-mass orbit is bound.
steps: Kinetic term is 1²/2=0.5.
Potential term is −0.6/1=−0.6.
ε=−0.1<0 in these units.
cases.solution: The two-body orbit is bound in this idealized instantaneous model; an actual binary also requires the correct post-event relative velocity and masses.

cases.title: Same energy, different shape
cases.scenario: Two point-mass binaries have identical m₁,m₂,a but eccentricities 0 and 0.7.
cases.task: Compare total energy, pericentre distance and angular momentum.
steps: Energy depends on a, not e: E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) for both.
Pericentre is a(1−e): a versus 0.3a.
Angular momentum magnitude at fixed a is proportional to sqrt(1−e²).
cases.solution: Same orbital energy does not mean same closest approach or same angular momentum; eccentricity determines the latter two.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Massive-star evolution and metallicity
sets.summary: Follow fuel burning, stellar winds, core collapse and metallicity-dependent pathways to remnants.

objectives.title: Build the stellar lifecycle
objectives.evidence: Differentiate main-sequence burning, post-main-sequence stages and compact-remnant formation.

questions.prompt: What powers a massive star throughout most of its main-sequence lifetime?
choices: A stable black-hole accretion disc.
Core hydrogen fusion.
Continuous helium fusion in the core from birth.
questions.hint: Name the defining nuclear-burning stage of the main sequence.
questions.feedback: Hydrogen fusion dominates the energy generation of main-sequence stars; later core burning stages follow after core hydrogen exhaustion.

questions.prompt: Why do more massive stars generally have shorter main-sequence lifetimes despite more fuel?
choices: Their initial hydrogen abundance is always zero.
Their luminosities and fuel-consumption rates increase strongly with mass.
They do not undergo hydrogen burning.
questions.hint: Compare available nuclear fuel with the rate of energy production.
questions.feedback: Main-sequence lifetime scales roughly as fuel divided by luminosity, and luminosity rises steeply with mass over much of the massive-star regime.

questions.prompt: A star's photospheric radius increases after it leaves the main sequence. Does that alone prove its helium core is already fusing?
choices: Yes; radius uniquely identifies the active core fuel.
No; shell burning and structural readjustment can expand the envelope before stable core helium ignition.
No; expansion always means no nuclear fusion anywhere.
questions.hint: Distinguish surface observables from the burning stage of the core.
questions.feedback: Post-main-sequence expansion can occur while hydrogen-shell burning supports luminosity; radius alone does not uniquely reveal central burning.

objectives.title: Compute timescale and mass budgets
objectives.evidence: Use mass-loss rates and dimensional reasoning without assuming a constant rate in a real star.

questions.prompt: A toy star loses 2 solar masses per million years for 3 million years at a constant rate. How much mass is lost?
choices: 2/3 solar mass.
6 solar masses.
1.5 solar masses.
questions.hint: Multiply rate by duration; this is a deliberately constant-rate toy model.
questions.feedback: ΔM=2 M☉/Myr ×3 Myr=6 M☉, assuming the rate is constant over the interval.

questions.prompt: If a star's luminosity is multiplied by 4 while its available nuclear fuel remains fixed, the fuel/L timescale becomes:
choices: Four times as long.
One quarter.
Unchanged.
questions.hint: Use timescale ≈ available energy / luminosity.
questions.feedback: With the same energy reservoir and four times the rate of release, the approximate timescale is divided by four.

questions.prompt: A star starts at 30 M☉, loses 8 M☉ in winds, then transfers 4 M☉ to its companion. Its remaining mass in this accounting toy model is:
questions.hint: Subtract both mass-loss channels from the initial mass.
questions.feedback: 30−8−4=18 M☉; real binary mass changes can also involve accretion and additional outflows.

objectives.title: Trace metallicity and wind effects
objectives.evidence: Explain conditional effects of line-driven winds and why metallicity is not a deterministic remnant label.

questions.prompt: Under otherwise comparable massive-star conditions, lower metallicity often weakens which mass-loss channel?
choices: Gravitational-wave emission from a single noncompact star.
Metal-line-driven stellar winds.
The definition of initial binary separation.
questions.hint: Recall that metallic absorption lines transfer radiative momentum to outer layers.
questions.feedback: Fewer heavy-element line absorbers often reduce line-driven wind efficiency, leaving more stellar mass available for later evolution under a specified model.

questions.prompt: Why is 'low metallicity guarantees a heavier black hole' too strong?
choices: Metallicity does not influence any wind model.
Binary interactions, rotation, explosion prescriptions and other mass-loss channels also influence the final remnant.
Every low-metallicity massive star collapses directly into a black hole of its birth mass.
questions.hint: Look for multiple evolutionary mechanisms affecting the final core and envelope.
questions.feedback: Metallicity can affect wind mass loss, but outcomes depend on initial mass, binary interaction, remnant prescriptions and other assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why must a population model track star-formation metallicity rather than only present-day metallicity?
choices: Every star changes its birth metallicity to the current cosmic mean.
Progenitors formed earlier under the metallicity distribution at their formation epoch.
Gravitational waves directly measure the host's birth metallicity without inference.
questions.hint: Merger time can be long after the binary formed.
questions.feedback: Compact binaries encode delayed stellar histories; their birth metallicity distribution can differ from the environment at merger time.

objectives.title: Critique stellar-to-remnant inference
objectives.evidence: Separate an observable, a simulation prescription and an uncertain inferred physical outcome.

questions.prompt: Two simulations give different black-hole masses from the same zero-age mass. What should be checked first?
choices: Which output filename is shorter.
Wind, mixing, binary-interaction and remnant-formation prescriptions.
Whether both simulations obey identical black-hole mass distributions by definition.
questions.hint: Compare assumptions and evolutionary histories, not just their final scalar output.
questions.feedback: Massive-star evolution depends on multiple prescriptions; differences do not alone identify which code or physics is correct.

questions.prompt: Can one infer a star's full evolution uniquely from one point on an H–R diagram?
choices: Yes; temperature and luminosity fix all historical parameters exactly.
No; multiple masses, ages and evolutionary tracks can occupy similar locations.
Only if distance is measured to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Consider age, composition, extinction and binary contamination.
questions.feedback: Luminosity and temperature are useful constraints but do not generally identify a unique evolutionary history.

questions.prompt: A toy calculation assigns every massive star the same wind mass loss independent of composition. What scientific question does it fail to explore?
choices: The number of rows in an output table.
Sensitivity of final masses to metallicity-dependent wind prescriptions.
Whether all stars have identical initial masses.
questions.hint: Ask which physical variable the prescription deliberately ignores.
questions.feedback: Holding mass loss constant across metallicity removes that pathway from the model and cannot test its impact on remnant populations.

cases.title: Two birth environments
cases.scenario: Two otherwise comparable toy massive stars start at 35 M☉. Model A loses 15 M☉ in winds and Model B loses 5 M☉.
cases.task: Calculate pre-collapse masses and explain why final remnant masses still cannot be read off directly.
steps: A has 20 M☉ remaining and B has 30 M☉ remaining.
Wind mass loss changes the pre-collapse budget.
Explosion, fallback, binary interaction and remnant prescription are unprovided.
cases.solution: The model suggests a possible effect of wind prescriptions, not a one-to-one black-hole mass prediction.

cases.title: Observed hot star
cases.scenario: An H–R diagram places a hot luminous star near two model tracks with different mass and binary histories.
cases.task: List evidence needed before assigning a unique progenitor path.
steps: Check observational uncertainties in luminosity/temperature and distance/extinction.
Inspect metallicity, rotation and possible binary contamination.
Compare multiple evolutionary tracks and quantify model uncertainty.
cases.solution: A single location in an H–R diagram constrains, but does not by itself uniquely reconstruct, stellar history.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Roche geometry and mass-transfer stability
sets.summary: Distinguish overflow onset, transfer rate, stability response and angular-momentum changes.

objectives.title: Identify when transfer begins
objectives.evidence: Connect Roche-lobe filling with binary separation and the donor's radius.

questions.prompt: What is the usual geometric trigger for Roche-lobe overflow in a binary model?
choices: The companion's radius must be exactly zero.
The donor expands to fill or overfill its Roche lobe.
The binary must first become unbound.
questions.hint: Compare donor radius with its effective Roche-lobe radius.
questions.feedback: Roche-lobe overflow begins when the donor fills its effective equipotential boundary, allowing material to pass toward its companion.

questions.prompt: Does filling a Roche lobe alone determine whether mass transfer is dynamically stable?
choices: Yes; all overflowing donors transfer stably forever.
No; compare how donor radius and Roche-lobe radius respond to mass loss.
Yes; every overflowing donor instantly enters a common envelope.
questions.hint: Onset geometry and dynamical stability are separate questions.
questions.feedback: Stability depends on structural response, orbital evolution, mass ratio and timescale, not on geometry alone.

questions.prompt: In the usual binary-star terminology, the donor is:
choices: Always the initially less massive star.
The star losing mass to the other component or out of the system.
The remnant formed at the end of every binary simulation.
questions.hint: Define the direction of mass exchange at the current episode.
questions.feedback: Donor and accretor identify instantaneous mass-transfer roles; roles may change in complex histories.

objectives.title: Calculate mass and orbit budgets
objectives.evidence: Apply simple conservative-transfer accounting before considering non-conservative loss.

questions.prompt: In a conservative transfer episode, donor mass drops from 10 to 8 M☉ and the companion began at 6 M☉. The companion ends at:
questions.hint: Mass lost by the donor is gained by the companion if the system loses none.
questions.feedback: The donor loses 2 M☉, so the accretor gains 2 M☉ and ends at 8 M☉.

questions.prompt: A donor loses 3 M☉; the companion gains 1 M☉. With no other mass changes, how much leaves the binary?
questions.hint: Subtract accreted material from donor mass loss.
questions.feedback: The remaining 2 M☉ leaves the modeled binary; this is non-conservative mass transfer.

questions.prompt: A 12 M☉ donor transfers 4 M☉ conservatively to a 5 M☉ companion. The final donor-to-accretor mass ratio is:
questions.hint: Update both masses before taking their ratio.
questions.feedback: The donor ends at 8 M☉ and companion at 9 M☉, so q=8/9 under this toy accounting.

objectives.title: Reason about stability and feedback
objectives.evidence: Compare donor shrinkage/expansion with Roche-lobe change and timescale.

questions.prompt: Suppose mass loss causes the donor to expand faster than its Roche lobe. What feedback can occur?
choices: Overflow necessarily stops immediately.
Overfilling grows and mass transfer can run away.
The Roche lobe ceases to exist.
questions.hint: Compare the two evolving radii rather than a fixed-radius snapshot.
questions.feedback: If donor radius increases relative to the Roche boundary, overflow deepens; the resulting runaway can occur on short timescales, depending on the model.

questions.prompt: Why can a convective-envelope giant be more vulnerable to unstable transfer in some mass-ratio regimes?
choices: Convective envelopes guarantee conservative transfer.
Its structural radius response to mass loss can worsen overflow.
Convection prevents all Roche-lobe overflow.
questions.hint: Think about the donor's response to rapid stripping.
questions.feedback: A donor's adiabatic radius response and the Roche-lobe response govern stability; extended convective giants can expand under rapid mass loss in relevant regimes.

questions.prompt: A binary changes its mass ratio during transfer. Why may the orbit's evolution change sign?
choices: The orbit has a fixed direction of change independent of initial masses.
Mass transfer redistributes masses and angular momentum; the orbital response depends on their evolving values.
Mass ratio cannot change during transfer.
questions.hint: Track the component masses and any angular momentum carried away.
questions.feedback: Conservative transfer and non-conservative outflows can shrink or widen an orbit under different mass ratios and angular-momentum prescriptions.

objectives.title: Inspect assumptions in a transfer model
objectives.evidence: Identify missing angular momentum, timescale or accretion efficiency assumptions.

questions.prompt: A simulation says 'stable transfer' but gives only the initial mass ratio. What else is needed to evaluate this claim?
choices: Only the initial component labels.
Donor evolutionary state, response to mass loss and Roche-lobe/orbital prescription.
A detector noise spectrum at merger.
questions.hint: Stability thresholds depend on stellar structure and response, not just q.
questions.feedback: Mass ratio is one input; stellar-envelope structure, timescales, accretion and angular-momentum loss can affect the stability criterion.

questions.prompt: A model assumes fully conservative transfer but its reported total binary mass decreases with no other process. What is the immediate issue?
choices: The star-formation history is always wrong.
Mass accounting contradicts the stated assumption.
Conservative transfer requires the donor and accretor to have equal mass.
questions.hint: Total mass is fixed during the idealized conservative transfer episode.
questions.feedback: Under genuinely conservative transfer with no other process, the donor's lost mass should equal the companion's gain.

questions.prompt: Two models predict different post-transfer separations. Which comparison can isolate the effect of angular-momentum loss?
choices: Change winds, kicks, transfer efficiency and initial binaries simultaneously.
Hold other assumptions fixed and vary the outflow's specific-angular-momentum prescription.
Ignore separation and compare only model names.
questions.hint: Use one-change-at-a-time sensitivity checks where possible.
questions.feedback: Changing multiple inputs at once confounds the physical cause; controlled model comparisons clarify parameter sensitivity.

cases.title: Mass-transfer ledger
cases.scenario: A 14 M☉ donor loses 5 M☉; a 9 M☉ companion accretes 3 M☉; all other changes are neglected.
cases.task: Compute final masses, mass lost to the surroundings and whether the episode is conservative.
steps: Donor: 14−5=9 M☉.
Companion: 9+3=12 M☉.
2 M☉ was not accreted and is lost to the surroundings.
cases.solution: The binary total decreases from 23 to 21 M☉; this is non-conservative transfer and its orbital impact additionally needs the angular momentum carried by escaping matter.

cases.title: Geometry versus stability
cases.scenario: A donor just fills its Roche lobe. A model predicts that after small mass loss its radius increases by 3% but its Roche radius increases by 1%.
cases.task: Predict the qualitative overflow response and name missing information.
steps: Donor radius grows relative to its Roche boundary.
Overflow therefore deepens in this local comparison.
Further stability analysis needs the response over appropriate timescales and the mass-transfer prescription.
cases.solution: The local response suggests positive feedback; it does not uniquely establish the eventual outcome from one step alone.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Common-envelope energetics and channels
sets.summary: Test drag, envelope binding, efficiency assumptions and why short-period survivors matter.

objectives.title: Describe the interaction
objectives.evidence: Distinguish common-envelope evolution from ordinary stable transfer.

questions.prompt: A common-envelope episode usually involves:
choices: Two unrelated stars separated by many parsecs.
A companion moving within a shared stellar envelope while drag exchanges orbital energy and angular momentum with gas.
A stable empty cavity that cannot exchange energy.
questions.hint: Look for the phase involving an envelope shared with the companion.
questions.feedback: Envelope gas can drain orbital energy and angular momentum, potentially ejecting gas and dramatically tightening the binary.

questions.prompt: Does a common-envelope episode necessarily end with two surviving compact remnants?
choices: Yes; every episode produces two black holes immediately.
No; the binary may merge during the envelope phase or emerge as a tighter noncompact/compact pair.
Yes; envelope ejection is guaranteed if the donor fills its lobe.
questions.hint: Consider ejection versus in-envelope merger and later stellar evolution.
questions.feedback: CE outcomes depend on envelope binding, energy transfer and stellar structure; any later compact-object formation is a separate evolutionary step.

questions.prompt: Which feature often motivates a common-envelope phase in compact-binary formation models?
choices: It turns the system into a three-body orbit by definition.
It can reduce orbital separation enough to enable a later merger within a cosmic time.
It removes the need for any subsequent supernova or remnant evolution.
questions.hint: Think about long inspiral times at large separation.
questions.feedback: Orbital tightening in some surviving systems can greatly shorten eventual gravitational-wave inspiral times.

objectives.title: Apply a simplified energy budget
objectives.evidence: Distinguish released orbital-energy magnitude from ejection efficiency and binding energy.

questions.prompt: In a toy energy formalism, an envelope needs 6 energy units to unbind and the usable fraction of released orbital energy is 0.5. What released energy is needed if no other source contributes?
choices: 3 units.
12 units.
6.5 units.
questions.hint: Solve α ΔE_release≥E_bind for ΔE_release.
questions.feedback: At efficiency α=0.5, at least 6/0.5=12 released-energy units are required under the model.

questions.prompt: If a binary's orbital energy changes from −4 to −10 units during shrinkage, the orbital energy released in magnitude is:
choices: −14 units.
6 units.
14 units.
questions.hint: Released energy is the drop in orbital energy magnitude: E_initial−E_final.
questions.feedback: The orbital energy decreases by 6 units, releasing 6 units to other degrees of freedom in this simplified account.

questions.prompt: A toy envelope's binding energy magnitude doubles at unchanged available released orbital energy and α. Ejection in the same energy-budget model becomes:
choices: Guaranteed to be easier.
More difficult.
Unaffected by binding energy.
questions.hint: Compare required energy with accessible energy.
questions.feedback: Doubling the required energy while holding supply fixed makes the toy inequality α ΔE_release≥E_bind harder to satisfy.

objectives.title: Trace orbital shrinkage and outcomes
objectives.evidence: Connect drag, available energy and post-envelope binary evolution.

questions.prompt: What is a direct channel by which an embedded companion can lose orbital energy?
choices: A compulsory increase in the companion's rest mass.
Dynamical interaction and drag with surrounding envelope gas.
The instantaneous absence of any force.
questions.hint: The envelope is not dynamically inert.
questions.feedback: The companion's motion through gas excites flows and transfers orbital energy and angular momentum into the envelope.

questions.prompt: If the envelope is ejected before the cores merge, the remnant binary is commonly:
choices: Forced to have exactly its initial separation.
Much more compact than before the interaction.
Always a pair of already formed black holes.
questions.hint: Think about the energy source used to help eject gas.
questions.feedback: Shrinking orbital separation can release orbital energy and leave a closer pair of stellar cores/remnants; later evolution is model-dependent.

questions.prompt: Why can stronger assumed envelope binding increase predicted merger-within-envelope outcomes?
choices: More binding energy guarantees that the envelope escapes spontaneously.
More orbital energy must be transferred before ejection, potentially requiring a smaller separation than survival allows.
Envelope binding energy is unrelated to any ejection model.
questions.hint: Think about competition between envelope ejection and core coalescence.
questions.feedback: In a simple budget, a more tightly bound envelope needs more accessible energy; the companion may spiral in too far before successful ejection.

objectives.title: Critique an efficiency prescription
objectives.evidence: Recognize that an energy parameter is an approximation rather than a directly observed universal constant.

questions.prompt: A model claims that a single chosen CE efficiency parameter is a measured universal constant for all stellar envelopes. What is the concern?
choices: The common-envelope concept cannot be modeled numerically.
The parameter is a simplified and uncertain prescription that may vary with system properties.
Efficiency automatically equals the donor-to-companion mass ratio.
questions.hint: Separate parameterized modeling from universal measurement.
questions.feedback: CE evolution is multidimensional and uncertain; one energy-efficiency parameter is not established as a universal measured constant.

questions.prompt: Can successful energy-budget ejection alone prove a realistic post-envelope binary survives?
choices: Yes; a positive energy budget guarantees no core collision.
No; final core radii, orbital separation and merger conditions also need checking.
No; conservation of energy is invalid for any binary.
questions.hint: Satisfying a necessary toy inequality may not be sufficient for physical survival.
questions.feedback: A model must also check whether the post-spiral-in separation accommodates the surviving objects and whether other losses occur.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a comparison of predicted merger rates under two CE prescriptions?
choices: Only the higher rate with no uncertainties.
A statement of the changed parameters and which other binary and cosmic assumptions were held fixed.
A claim that both outputs are direct measurements of the real Universe.
questions.hint: Rates mix binary-physics assumptions with population weighting and cosmic history.
questions.feedback: Documenting assumptions and controlled variations is essential to interpret an uncertain evolutionary pathway.

cases.title: Envelope energy audit
cases.scenario: A toy CE event has |E_bind|=10 units, ΔE_release=15 units and α=0.6, with no other energy source.
cases.task: Does the elementary budget predict enough usable energy for ejection, and what does it not establish?
steps: Available useful energy =0.6×15=9 units.
9<10, so this toy budget does not reach the required envelope binding energy.
Other physical energy sources and hydrodynamic outcomes are outside the simplified model.
cases.solution: The simple α-energy budget fails its ejection inequality; this alone cannot establish the physical result of a complete hydrodynamic CE simulation.

cases.title: Outcome dependence
cases.scenario: Two models use the same pre-CE binary but assign different donor envelope binding energies.
cases.task: State a controlled comparison and two outcomes to track.
steps: Hold initial masses, separation and other prescriptions fixed.
Vary only binding-energy evaluation or efficiency.
Record ejected envelope versus core merger and surviving post-CE separation.
cases.solution: The experiment identifies sensitivity to CE energetics without claiming that one prescription is observationally proven.
